Question B-007-005-001.

Why the correct answer is right: Sunspots are a visible sign of stronger solar magnetic activity. When the sunspot count is higher, the Sun usually sends more ionizing radiation toward Earth, so the upper atmosphere contains more free electrons for HF refraction.

Why the distractors are wrong:
- sourceIndex 1: "The more sunspots there are, the lesser the ionization": That reverses the usual relationship; higher sunspot activity raises, rather than lowers, ionization in the reflecting regions.
- sourceIndex 2: "Unless there are sunspots, the ionization is zero": Daylight still ionizes the atmosphere when no sunspots are visible, so low solar activity does not mean a completely neutral ionosphere.
- sourceIndex 3: "They have no effect": Sunspots are one of the standard indicators operators use because they track solar activity that changes ionospheric conditions.
